questions.stem: An engineer put the team's TypeScript conventions in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Teammates report that Claude Code ignores those conventions on their machines. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is user-level memory that lives only on that engineer's machine. Move the team conventions into the project's CLAUDE.md (repo root or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`) and commit it.
options.why: User-level memory isn't shared through version control. Project memory is.

options.text: The file must be named `claude.md` in lower case.
options.why: The filename is `CLAUDE.md`. Case isn't the issue.

options.text: Teammates must run `/compact` to load the new file.
options.why: `/compact` summarises context. It doesn't load memory files.

options.text: CLAUDE.md is only read in plan mode.
options.why: False. Memory files load at session start in every mode.

questions.explanation: User scope (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) is personal. Team conventions belong in project-scoped CLAUDE.md committed to the repo.

questions.stem: Testing conventions apply to every `*.test.ts` and `*.spec.tsx` file, and those files are scattered across 40 directories. What is the most maintainable way to have Claude Code apply the conventions only when they are relevant?

options.text: Create a rule file in `.claude/rules/` with YAML frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.test.ts", "**/*.spec.tsx"]` containing the testing conventions.
options.why: Path-scoped rules load conditionally whenever matching files are being worked on, wherever they live.

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md to each of the 40 directories.
options.why: This duplicates content and is hard to maintain. New directories would be missed.

options.text: Put the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md under a "Testing" heading.
options.why: They would always be loaded, which wastes context, and their relevance would rely on inference.

options.text: Create a `/testing` skill and tell engineers to invoke it.
options.why: Skills need invocation, so the conventions wouldn't apply automatically.

questions.explanation: Use `.claude/rules/` with `paths:` globs for conventions that cut across the directory structure. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files suit conventions that follow the directory tree.

questions.stem: The platform team wants every engineer to have a `/new-endpoint` command that scaffolds an API route following house conventions. Where should it live?

options.text: `.claude/commands/new-endpoint.md` in the repository, committed to version control.
options.why: Project-scoped commands are shared with everyone who clones the repo.

options.text: `~/.claude/commands/new-endpoint.md` on each engineer's machine.
options.why: That is personal scope, and it would have to be copied and kept in sync by hand.

options.text: In the root CLAUDE.md under a `## Commands` heading.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is memory and instructions. It doesn't define slash commands.

options.text: In `.claude/commands.json` as a JSON array of command definitions.
options.why: No such configuration file exists.

questions.explanation: Shared slash commands go in the project's `.claude/commands/` directory. Personal ones go in `~/.claude/commands/`.

questions.stem: A `/audit-deps` skill reads hundreds of lockfile entries and produces a short report. Engineers say their main session context fills up after running it. Which SKILL.md frontmatter setting best addresses this?

options.text: `context: fork`, so the skill runs in an isolated sub-context and only its result returns to the main conversation.
options.why: Forked context isolates verbose work from the main session.

options.text: `allowed-tools: Read`
options.why: This restricts which tools the skill can use. It doesn't isolate context.

options.text: `argument-hint: <package>`
options.why: This only documents the expected arguments.

options.text: `model: small`
options.why: It doesn't address where the verbose output accumulates.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` runs a skill in its own context so that verbose intermediate work doesn't pollute the caller's session.

questions.stem: An engineer must migrate 120 files from a deprecated logging library to a new one, which involves choosing between two adapter strategies. What is the best way to use Claude Code?

options.text: Start in plan mode to explore usage patterns and agree on a strategy and migration plan, then switch to direct execution to implement it in batches.
options.why: Large, multi-file work with an architectural choice benefits from planning before execution.

options.text: Use direct execution and ask Claude to "migrate everything" in one prompt.
options.why: This is risky at scale, and the strategy choice would be made implicitly.

options.text: Use plan mode for the whole migration, including the edits.
options.why: Plan mode is for investigation and design. Implementation happens in execution.

options.text: Write a sed script instead, because Claude Code isn't suited to large changes.
options.why: This ignores the semantic differences between the libraries.

questions.explanation: Use plan mode for large-scale or architectural work and for choosing between approaches, then direct execution for the changes. Simple, well-scoped edits go straight to execution.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to rename a misspelled local variable in one function. Which mode fits best?

options.text: Direct execution. The change is small and well scoped.
options.why: Planning overhead isn't justified for a trivial, clear edit.

options.text: Plan mode, so Claude can explore the whole repo first.
options.why: That's overkill for a local rename.

options.text: An Explore subagent followed by plan mode.
options.why: This is unnecessary indirection for a one-line change.

options.text: A forked session, so the change is isolated.
options.why: A fork adds nothing for this task.

questions.explanation: Match the mode to the task: direct execution for simple, well-scoped changes.

questions.stem: Claude Code seems to follow an outdated convention, and the engineer suspects an old memory file is being loaded from somewhere. What is the fastest way to find out which memory files are in effect?

options.text: Run `/memory` to see which memory files are loaded and open them for editing.
options.why: `/memory` is the built-in way to inspect and edit loaded memory.

options.text: Run `/compact` and read the summary.
options.why: `/compact` compresses conversation history. It doesn't list memory sources.

options.text: Delete every CLAUDE.md in the repo and recreate them.
options.why: This is destructive guesswork.

options.text: Start Claude Code with `--verbose-memory`.
options.why: That flag doesn't exist.

questions.explanation: `/memory` shows the loaded memory hierarchy and is the standard diagnostic.

questions.stem: The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines covering API style, Terraform, frontend and release processes. What is the best restructuring?

options.text: Split it into focused files. Pull shared essentials into CLAUDE.md with `@path` imports, and move area-specific conventions into `.claude/rules/` files (path-scoped where appropriate) or subdirectory CLAUDE.md files.
options.why: Modular organisation keeps always-loaded context small and relevant.

options.text: Keep one file but make it more concise by removing examples.
options.why: Examples often carry the most value, and the file would still be monolithic.

options.text: Move everything into user-level memory to keep the repo clean.
options.why: Team conventions would no longer be shared.

options.text: Convert every section into a skill.
options.why: Skills are on-demand, so conventions that must always apply would be missed.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md supports modular organisation through `@import`, `.claude/rules/` and directory-level files. Keep what is always loaded lean.

questions.stem: Claude keeps generating date-formatting helpers that don't match the team's expectations, despite prose descriptions of the rules. What is the most effective refinement technique?

options.text: Provide 2–3 concrete input → expected-output examples (or failing tests) that capture the edge cases, then iterate against them.
options.why: Concrete examples and test-driven iteration remove the ambiguity that prose leaves.

options.text: Repeat the prose rules in capital letters.
options.why: Emphasis doesn't resolve ambiguity.

options.text: Ask Claude to "think harder" each time.
options.why: It still doesn't know the expected behaviour.

options.text: Switch models and try again.
options.why: This doesn't address the specification gap.

questions.explanation: Iterative refinement works best with concrete examples and tests. The interview pattern, where Claude asks clarifying questions, also helps with ambiguous requirements.

questions.stem: After two hours of exploring the billing module, Claude Code's answers are getting vague and it is forgetting earlier findings. The engineer still needs to implement a change. What should they do?

options.text: Have Claude write the key findings to a scratchpad or notes file (or use `/compact`), then continue from that summary, or start a fresh session that reads it.
options.why: Persisting findings and compacting counters context degradation in long sessions.

options.text: Keep going. The model will recover once it reaches the implementation step.
options.why: Degradation compounds in long sessions.

options.text: Paste the whole billing module into the chat so it's fresh.
options.why: This adds bloat and makes the problem worse.

options.text: Lower the temperature setting.
options.why: That has nothing to do with context degradation.

questions.explanation: In long explorations, persist findings (scratchpad files), compact or summarise, and continue in a fresh context.

questions.stem: Before changing the auth flow, an engineer wants Claude to survey how 30 services call the auth library, without the main session filling up with grep output. What is the best approach?

options.text: Delegate the survey to a subagent (for example the Explore subagent), which explores in its own context and returns a concise structured summary.
options.why: Subagent delegation isolates verbose discovery from the main context.

options.text: Run the greps in the main session and then run `/compact`.
options.why: This works, but it pollutes the context first and loses detail during compaction.

options.text: Ask Claude to read all 30 services in full.
options.why: This is maximum context bloat.

options.text: Skip the survey and change the library directly.
options.why: This is risky without understanding the call sites.

questions.explanation: Use subagents to explore and summarise, so the main session keeps the essential findings.

questions.stem: Yesterday an engineer worked in a named Claude Code session on a feature. Overnight, a teammate merged a large refactor that touched the same files. What is the best way to continue?

options.text: Start a fresh session seeded with a structured summary of yesterday's decisions, or resume and explicitly tell Claude which files changed so it re-reads them, rather than relying on stale tool results.
options.why: Resumed sessions can hold stale file contents. Fresh context with a summary is more reliable after big changes.

options.text: `--resume` the session and continue as if nothing changed.
options.why: Claude would reason from outdated file contents.

options.text: Fork the session so the old one is preserved.
options.why: A fork still inherits the stale context.

options.text: Revert the teammate's refactor locally to match the session state.
options.why: This works against the team.

questions.explanation: `--resume` is convenient, but after significant external changes either tell the session what changed or start fresh with a structured summary.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to try two competing implementations of a caching layer from the same point in a session, without either attempt contaminating the other's context. Which feature fits?

options.text: Fork the session (for example `--fork-session` with `--resume`, or `fork_session` in the SDK), so each branch starts from the same history and diverges independently.
options.why: Forking creates independent branches from a shared starting point.

options.text: Run `/compact` between attempts.
options.why: Compaction still carries attempt A's reasoning into attempt B.

options.text: Use plan mode for one attempt and execution for the other.
options.why: Modes don't isolate context.

options.text: Open a second terminal with a brand-new session and re-explain everything.
options.why: This works but loses the shared exploration history. Forking is the intended tool.

questions.explanation: Session forking explores alternatives from a common baseline.

questions.stem: The team wants every engineer's Claude Code to connect to the company's issue-tracker MCP server, but each engineer has their own API token. How should this be configured?

options.text: Commit a project-scoped `.mcp.json` that defines the server and references the token through environment-variable expansion, such as `${TRACKER_TOKEN}`. Each engineer sets the variable locally.
options.why: Shared config plus per-user secrets via env expansion is the standard pattern.

options.text: Commit `.mcp.json` with a shared service token written in plain text.
options.why: This leaks a secret into version control.

options.text: Have each engineer add the server to their user-level `~/.claude.json` by hand.
options.why: It works, but the shared config isn't version-controlled or consistent.

options.text: Put the server URL and token in CLAUDE.md.
options.why: CLAUDE.md isn't MCP configuration, and the token would leak.

questions.explanation: Project scope (`.mcp.json`) is for shared servers and user scope (`~/.claude.json`) is for personal ones. Use `${ENV_VAR}` expansion for secrets.

questions.stem: A multi-hour, multi-phase codebase modernisation keeps losing its place when the session crashes or the context is compacted. Which TWO practices make the work resumable? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Keep a manifest file listing each phase or file with its status (pending, done, failed) that Claude updates as it goes and reads on restart.
options.why: Manifest-based recovery makes progress durable outside the context window.

options.text: Summarise each completed phase into a notes file before spawning the next phase.
options.why: Summarising before each phase carries the essential state forward compactly.

options.text: Never let the session compact, by increasing the max output tokens.
options.why: Output tokens don't control context size.

options.text: Keep every phase in one ever-growing conversation for continuity.
options.why: That is exactly what causes degradation and fragility.

options.text: Rely on `--resume` to restore everything after a crash.
options.why: Resume restores the conversation, not a reliable progress ledger, and it may carry stale state.

questions.explanation: Durable external state (manifests, notes) plus phase summaries make long-running work robust.

questions.stem: An engineer likes a more verbose variant of the team's shared `/review` skill. What is the correct way to have a personal variant without affecting teammates?

options.text: Create a personal skill under `~/.claude/skills/` with a different name (for example `review-verbose`), leaving the shared project skill unchanged.
options.why: Personal variants under distinct names avoid conflicting with the team's shared skill.

options.text: Edit the shared skill in `.claude/skills/` and commit it.
options.why: This changes it for everyone.

options.text: Create a personal skill with the same name so it overrides the team's.
options.why: The same name creates ambiguity and conflicts. Use a distinct name.

options.text: Add "be verbose when I run /review" to the root CLAUDE.md.
options.why: That affects the whole team and bloats always-loaded memory.

questions.explanation: Keep personal customisations in user scope under distinct names. Project scope is for shared team assets.
